newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish inflation seen remaining at high levels.
newsitem.headline: Turkish inflation seen remaining at high levels.

text.p: Turkey's annual inflation is likely to remain over 70 percent in 1997 because of a lack of reforms by the troubled Islamist-led government, analysts said on Monday.

The State Institute of Statistics announced on Sunday consumer prices rose 6.6 percent month-on-month in April after a rise of 5.4 percent in March and were up 77.2 percent from a year earlier, compared with 77.3 percent the previous month.
Analysts forecast that prices would hold around these levels, or even rise, because of doubts about the future of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's 10-month-old government.
"Political instability has not decreased and inflation will continue to increase," said Oner Ayan, responsible for international capital markets at Ata Securities.
Last week, Erbakan blamed problems with the coalition's economic plans on an "artificial political crisis" -- a reference to a row with the military over Islamist activism.
April consumer price increases were higher than market forecasts of a 5.0-5.5 percent rise. Shares in Istanbul ended the morning session down 1.96 percent.
"The inflation figures came out higher than expected. They have had a negative impact on the stock market," said Nazmi Sarikaya of Dis Securities.

One banker said the consumer price inflation was offset by considerably lower wholesale price inflation. Wholesale prices rose 5.5 percent month-on-month in April, compared with a rise of 6.0 percent in March and were up 72.8 percent year-on-year, compared with 77.0 percent in March.
The government's aim of bringing annual inflation down to 57 percent in 1997 looks increasingly unlikely, according to analysts.
"We expect the end-1997 wholesale price inflation to stand at around 72.8 percent," said Altug Karamenderes, an economist at Ata Securities. Estimates ranged between 72 and 80 percent.

Despite the approach of the summer season, which usually heralds lower inflation in Turkey, there remained concerns among some analysts about demand-induced inflation, fuelled by an increase in money supply and public sector price hikes.

Confidence in the coalition's ability to meet its economic targets and push through reforms to ease pressure on public finances has been undermined by recent indications from Erbakan of problems in balancing the 1997 budget as planned.
The budget showed a deficit in 1996 of 1,217 trillion lira ($9 billion) and economists predict the deficit may exceed 1,500 trillion lira ($11 billion) in 1997.
Economists warn that unless steps are taken to cut the huge public sector borrowing requirement, which was 9.4 percent of GNP last year, there is little chance of fighting inflation.
